prize_parts.citation: For showing that liquid-liquid phase separation of multivalent biomolecules organizes the interior of living cells into membraneless compartments

statement.case_for: Biomolecular phase separation brought a general thermodynamic concept, demixing of multivalent macromolecules above a threshold concentration, into cell biology, and it did so with quantitative support: liquid-like P granules and nucleoli (Hyman, Brangwynne) and defined in vitro multivalent systems with phase diagrams (Rosen). It changed how a whole community thinks about intracellular organization, it is a physical-chemical idea at its core, and it has been reproduced across many systems and labs. It is a new way of thinking about molecular organization, which is what the Chemistry prize should reward, and it would show that physical chemistry and the chemistry of life are represented alongside synthesis and drug-discovery chemistry.
statement.case_against: This is the candidate where my own field makes me most likely to be generous, so I should state the weakness plainly. The field is still arguing over which reported condensates are true thermodynamic phase separation and which are overexpression artefacts or other assemblies, and the physiological role of many condensates is not settled. Attribution is also crowded: Pappu and Mittag are central on sequence grammar and physics, so a three-person cut is contestable, and the award could look early next to candidates with decades of validation or approved products.

responses.point: Linke ranks phase separation first, citing a clear physical principle (demixing, surface tension, concentration thresholds) with quantitative support, while noting that the physiological role versus overexpression artefacts is still debated.
responses.response: I agree on the principle and on the caveat, and I think the caveat bears on the citation rather than the candidacy. The citation should honour the demonstrated physical concept (liquid-like demixing as an organizing mechanism) and not claim that every reported condensate is a phase-separated body. I would also press the question of whether Rosen or Pappu and Mittag carry the quantitative physical-chemistry side best, since that decides who stands next to Hyman and Brangwynne. We are both from Lund, which makes it worth saying that I do not want agreement between us to count as independent confirmation.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks degraders first as a game-changer with real consequences, and says the PROTAC concept and the structure-guided VHL ligand work form a coherent Crews-Deshaies-Ciulli trio, while placing perovskites, sequencing and machine-learned potentials above phase separation.
responses.response: I take the real-consequences standard seriously, and degraders meet it as a new pharmacological modality. My reservations are about timing and the glue branch, not the chemistry: no PROTAC is approved, and the Handa-Ito cereblon story is a separate strand that a Crews-Deshaies-Ciulli citation would leave out. I would ask whether the committee prefers a mature, validated advance over a concept that is still being clinically tested. Phase separation is less clinical but already shapes how thousands of labs frame cellular organization. I do not claim it is more consequential than degraders, only that its maturity risk is of a different kind, scientific interpretation instead of clinical outcome.

responses.point: Aili ranks degraders first and base editing second, arguing that induced proximity is a general design principle that makes undruggable targets addressable, and that the 2020 CRISPR prize is a novelty question for base editing.
responses.response: I agree that induced proximity is a real design principle, and the shared interest in self-assembly and biointerfaces means we may weigh molecular organization similarly. Two qualifications. A prize for degraders has to decide between the PROTAC and molecular-glue lineages, and the three-name limit forces a cut Handa, Ito, Gray, Sakamoto and Kim could reasonably contest. On base editing I share your 2020 concern, which is why I rank it below lipid nanoparticles in my own opening. If the committee wants a medicine-adjacent chemistry prize this year, I would like to hear why degraders are more mature than the lipid nanoparticle work, which already underlies licensed products.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Pd-catalyzed C-N coupling first as a mature, general, conceptually simple method that is routine in medicinal and process chemistry, with the Buchwald-Hartwig credit clean and the 2010 cross-coupling prize only a minor overlap.
responses.response: I do not dispute the maturity or the Buchwald-Hartwig attribution. It is the safest candidate on the list for those reasons. My hesitation is conceptual rather than technical: it is a very important extension of cross-coupling, and the 2010 prize already honoured the Pd-catalysed disconnection logic, so the novelty margin is thinner than for a new organizing concept. I would welcome a sharper argument from you on what is genuinely new in C-N coupling beyond that 2010 prize. I would not oppose it as an alternative if the committee prefers certainty over novelty, but I would not rank it above phase separation.

uncertainties: How much of the reported in-cell condensate literature reflects true thermodynamic phase separation, and whether that weakens a prize now or only the wording of the citation
Whether the cut should be Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen, or whether Pappu or Mittag must replace Rosen to carry the physical-chemistry side
Whether the committee will see degraders (B067) as ready, given no approved PROTAC and the unresolved PROTAC versus molecular-glue split
Whether the 2023 Medicine prize for nucleoside modification and the 2020 CRISPR prize reduce the standing of B047 and B052 for a Chemistry award
statement.conflict_note: No personal or institutional connection to any candidate on the shortlist is apparent from my profile. My research on lipid self-assembly and amyloid is scientifically close to B049 and B047, so I have a field bias that I should be explicit about, but it is not a recusal issue. Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai are Lund colleagues, and Daniel Aili and Peter Brzezinski work in overlapping areas; none of these relationships is a conflict with a candidate.
